Sumar un vector a un punto lo desplaza;: Adding a vector to a point shifts it; multiplying its coordinates by $k$ is the similarity of scale factor $k$; and a $2\times 2$ matrix turns every vector into another. This topic brings those three ideas together under one name, transformation, and classifies the ones that do not distort. It is where the geometry of the plane and the matrices of the algebra block recognise each other.
Una <strong>transformación</strong> conv: A transformation turns every point of the plane into another point. The most important are the ones that do not distort: they preserve distances, and therefore angles and areas too. They are called isometries.

Cada vez que arrastras, giras o amplías: Every time you drag, turn or zoom something on a screen one of these transformations is being applied to thousands of points at once. Image editors, design programs and video games store them as matrices and chain them by multiplying, which is exactly what you will see in the linear algebra block. The animation of a film is a succession of transformations applied to a model.

Clasificar los movimientos del plano fue: Classifying the isometries of the plane was the seed of an enormous idea. In 1872, Felix Klein proposed in his Erlangen Programme defining each geometry by the group of transformations leaving its properties unchanged. Euclidean geometry is the one of isometries; if you also admit enlargements you get affine geometry; and so on up to topology, where any continuous deformation is allowed. The same figure is “the same” or not according to which transformations you consider legal.
